prompt: What separates a LAN from a WAN, in this lesson's sense?
hint: Think about who sends the bill.

choices.text: How many machines are connected
choices.why: A LAN can hold a few machines or thousands. The count is not what decides.

choices.text: Who owns the links
choices.why: Right. A LAN is built from equipment the company owns; a WAN's links belong to a provider.

choices.text: Whether the machines use Wi-Fi or cables
choices.why: The company's own Wi-Fi is part of its LAN, bridged to the same Ethernet.

choices.text: The speed printed on the switch ports
choices.why: Speed follows from ownership, and a WAN link can be fast; it does not define the category.

prompt: pc1's table holds `10.20.10.0/24 dev eth0 ... scope link` and `default via 10.20.10.1`. Where does pc1 send a packet for 10.20.10.200?
hint: Which of the two lines covers .200?

choices.text: To rhq at 10.20.10.1, which forwards it
choices.why: The default route is for addresses no other line covers, and 10.20.10.0/24 covers this one.

choices.text: To the provider, through rhq
choices.why: Nothing in pc1's table names the provider; even the default route stops at rhq.

choices.text: Nowhere, since nobody has that address
choices.why: pc1 cannot know that in advance. It asks with ARP, and a silence is the answer it may get.

choices.text: Onto its own cable, via ARP
choices.why: Right. 10.20.10.200 is inside 10.20.10.0/24, pc1's LAN, which is reached directly.

prompt: In pc1's routing table, the line that hands everything outside its LAN to rhq begins with the word ___.
Which of these are LANs in this lesson's sense? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The head office's 10.20.10.0/24
choices.why: Right: the company's own switch and cables, reached directly.

choices.text: A line to the building across the street, rented from a provider
choices.why: Short, but the link belongs to the provider: a WAN link.

choices.text: Three buildings of one campus joined by fibre the company owns
choices.why: Right: a distance does not turn the company's own network into a WAN.

choices.text: 203.0.113.0/30, between rhq and isp
choices.why: That is the link the provider sold to the head office.

choices.text: The branch's Wi-Fi, from access points the company installed
choices.why: Right: the access points bridge the radio onto the same LAN.

prompt: isp's routing table holds only 198.51.100.0/30 and 203.0.113.0/30. Why is there no route to 10.30.10.0/24?
hint: Who else uses addresses that start with 10?

choices.text: Providers do not route private addresses
choices.why: Right. Thousands of companies use the same private ranges, so no provider could know which one is meant.

choices.text: The branch router has not been switched on yet
choices.why: rbr answered the traceroute at 198.51.100.2, so it is on.

choices.text: The lab forgot to start OSPF on isp
choices.why: The sites scenario runs no routing protocol at all, and a provider would refuse these routes anyway.

choices.text: The route expired after the traceroute finished
choices.why: A traceroute adds and removes no route; isp never had one.

prompt: pc1's traceroute to 198.51.100.2 worked although isp has no route to 10.20.10.0/24. How did the replies get back?
hint: What does the head office look like from the WAN?

choices.text: isp learnt the route while the traceroute ran
choices.why: isp's table, read after the traceroute, still has only its two links.

choices.text: rhq swapped pc1's address for its public one, 203.0.113.2
choices.why: Right. The replies were addressed to 203.0.113.2, which isp reaches directly, and rhq handed them to pc1. That is NAT, lesson 11.

choices.text: Replies are broadcast to every network
choices.why: Routers do not forward broadcasts, and a reply has one destination.

choices.text: The branch router sent them through the tunnel
choices.why: The tunnel did not exist yet; the VPN section builds it later in the lesson.

prompt: Match each kind of WAN link to what the company is buying.
hint: Three kinds, from dedicated to shared.

pairs.right: A dedicated circuit, the same capacity day and night
A provider's network that keeps several customers' traffic apart
An ordinary connection at each site, joined by a tunnel

right_distractors: A switch port in the company's cupboard

prompt: How many addresses does a /30 link such as 203.0.113.0/30 hold, counting both ends and the two that are not used by a device?
hint: The section says it of each WAN link.

prompt: A company rents metro Ethernet between two of its buildings in the same city. Seen from the company, what is that link?

choices.text: A LAN, because it carries Ethernet
choices.why: The frames are Ethernet, and the link is still rented. Ownership decides.

choices.text: A VLAN of the provider's switch
choices.why: A VLAN divides a switch; it says nothing about who owns the fibre.

choices.text: A short WAN link
choices.why: Right. The provider owns it and bills for it; the short distance does not change that.

choices.text: A VPN between the buildings
choices.why: A VPN is a tunnel inside packets. Metro Ethernet delivers frames directly.

prompt: In what shape do providers lay fibre round a city, and what does it buy them?

choices.text: A bus, which needs the least fibre
choices.why: A bus fails as a whole at one break, the opposite of what a city's customers pay for.

choices.text: A full mesh between every pair of buildings
choices.why: With hundreds of buildings, n × (n − 1) / 2 runs of fibre is out of reach.

choices.text: A star around the provider's own building
choices.why: Then each customer would depend on one run of fibre with no second way.

choices.text: A ring, so a cut still leaves a way out
choices.why: Right. Every building on a ring has two ways out, at one run of fibre per building.

prompt: The standards body behind Ethernet and Wi-Fi is the IEEE 802 LAN/___ Standards Committee.
pc1 is in VLAN 10 and pc2 in VLAN 20, on adjacent ports of one switch. What does pc1 need to reach pc2?

choices.text: Nothing, since they share a switch
choices.why: Sharing the hardware is the point of a VLAN, and the switch still keeps them apart.

choices.text: A cable straight from pc1 to pc2, outside the switch
choices.why: That builds a third network beside the switch; it does not join the two VLANs.

choices.text: A router between the two VLANs
choices.why: Right. The switch forwards frames only inside a VLAN, so crossing between them is a router's job (lesson 22).

choices.text: A VPN between the two ports
choices.why: A VPN joins networks across somebody else's network. Two ports of one switch need a router.

prompt: A PC in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request to the broadcast address. Which ports of the switch deliver it?
hint: A VLAN is a broadcast boundary.

choices.text: Every port of the switch, since it is a broadcast
choices.why: A broadcast fills its own VLAN and stops at the edge of it.

choices.text: The router's port alone
choices.why: ARP asks every machine on the LAN; the router is one of them, not the only one.

choices.text: None, because VLANs drop ARP
choices.why: Without ARP no machine in the VLAN could reach another. VLANs limit broadcasts; they do not drop them.

choices.text: The other ports in VLAN 10
choices.why: Right. Broadcasts stay inside their VLAN, which is half of why VLANs exist.

prompt: How many bytes long is the 802.1Q tag that marks a frame's VLAN on a trunk?
hint: The section names it; lesson 19 opens it.

prompt: Before the tunnel, pc1's ping to 10.30.10.22 printed `From 203.0.113.1 icmp_seq=1 Destination Net Unreachable`. Which device sent that message?

choices.text: rbr, the branch router
choices.why: The packet never reached rbr; it died one router earlier.

choices.text: pc1 itself, before sending anything
choices.why: When pc1 refuses on its own it prints Network is unreachable, without a From.

choices.text: isp, the provider's router
choices.why: Right. 203.0.113.1 is the provider's end of the head office's link, and it has no route to the branch's LAN.

choices.text: pc2, which refused the ping
choices.why: pc2 is never reached, and its address is 10.30.10.22.

prompt: Through the tunnel, the reply from pc2 arrives with `ttl=62`. Which routers each took one from the inner packet's TTL?

choices.text: rbr and rhq
choices.why: Right. 64 minus the two routers that forwarded the inner packet is 62.

choices.text: rbr, isp and rhq
choices.why: That would leave 61. isp forwards the outer packet and never sees the inner TTL.

choices.text: isp alone, twice
choices.why: isp forwards the encrypted outer packet and cannot read the inner one at all.

choices.text: No router; pc2 sends 62
choices.why: A Linux machine starts at 64, as the ring and the office captures show.

prompt: On rhq, `wg set wg0 ... peer +JFz… endpoint 198.51.100.2:51820 allowed-ips 10.30.10.0/24,10.255.255.2/32`. What does allowed-ips decide?

choices.text: Which public addresses may open a connection to port 51820
choices.why: The outer side is the endpoint. allowed-ips is about the packets inside the tunnel.

choices.text: Which head office PCs may use the tunnel
choices.why: It names the branch's addresses, not the head office's.

choices.text: Which addresses the provider is allowed to route
choices.why: The provider is never told about the tunnel's inner addresses.

choices.text: Which inner source addresses this peer may send from
choices.why: Right. Packets arriving from the branch must come from 10.30.10.0/24 or 10.255.255.2, and nothing else is accepted.

prompt: Put the head office router's configuration in the order it was typed.
items: Give it a port, a private key and the branch as its peer
Give wg0 its address and bring it up
Route the branch's LAN into wg0
trap: The interface has to exist before `wg set` can configure it, and the route goes last because it points at wg0.

prompt: The two private keys of the lab's tunnel are written in lab.sh. What follows for a real tunnel?

choices.text: They are safe, since wg show prints them as hidden
choices.why: wg show hides the key on the screen; the file still has it for anybody to read.

choices.text: Make new ones with wg genkey: a printed key protects nothing
choices.why: Right. A private key that anybody can read is not private, and those keys are in a public file on purpose.

choices.text: They work as long as the endpoints change
choices.why: The endpoint is an address; it does not make a leaked key secret again.

choices.text: Replace the public keys and keep the private ones
choices.why: The public keys are meant to be shared. It is the private ones that leaked.

prompt: While pc1 pinged pc2 through the tunnel, what could the provider read on isp's cable? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the first tcpdump line by line.

choices.text: The two routers' public addresses
choices.why: Right: 203.0.113.2 and 198.51.100.2 are in every line.

choices.text: pc1's address, 10.20.10.21
choices.why: Inner addresses are encrypted; they appear only on wg0.

choices.text: The UDP port, 51820
choices.why: Right: the port is in the outer header, in clear.

choices.text: That the packets were ICMP echo requests
choices.why: The word ICMP is only in the capture inside the tunnel.

choices.text: The size of each datagram, 128
choices.why: Right: length 128 is printed for all four, and a bigger packet would show a bigger number.

prompt: A ping packet of 84 bytes is padded to 96 and encrypted, and WireGuard adds a 16-byte header and a 16-byte tag. What UDP length does tcpdump print?
Who can read the pings between pc1 and pc2 in clear?

choices.text: Anybody listening on the provider's cable
choices.why: That is the first capture: two public addresses, a port and a size.

choices.text: pc1 alone
choices.why: pc2 reads them too, and so does anybody on either router.

choices.text: Whoever controls rhq, rbr, pc1 or pc2
choices.why: Right. Encryption covers the path between the routers; at either end the traffic is in clear, as wg0 showed.

choices.text: Nobody, not even pc2
choices.why: pc2 has to read the ping to answer it.

prompt: Why does tcpdump on rhq's wg0 print `link-type RAW (Raw IP)`?
hint: What would an Ethernet header hold?

choices.text: tcpdump could not decrypt the packets
choices.why: On wg0 the packets are already decrypted; the ICMP is readable.

choices.text: A tunnel carries bare IP, with no MAC addresses
choices.why: Right. There is no link with hardware addresses inside a tunnel, so there is nothing for an Ethernet header to say.

choices.text: The capture was taken on the provider's side
choices.why: That capture was on isp's eth0 and printed link-type EN10MB (Ethernet).

choices.text: WireGuard removes the Ethernet header to save space
choices.why: There was never an Ethernet header on wg0 to remove.

prompt: Match each word to where it appears in this lesson's lab.
hint: The figure in the LAN section.

prompt: A branch says its tunnel is up. A capture on the branch router's internet side shows ICMP from 10.30.10.22 to 10.20.10.21. What does that tell you?
hint: What did the capture on isp show when the tunnel worked?

choices.text: It bypasses the tunnel, in clear
choices.why: Right. Through the tunnel the outside shows only UDP between public addresses; private ICMP there means a path that skips it.

choices.text: The tunnel is working as intended
choices.why: A working tunnel shows UDP 51820 on the outside, as on isp.

choices.text: The provider has decrypted the traffic
choices.why: A provider has no key. The capture is on the branch's own router.

choices.text: The capture was taken on wg0 by mistake
choices.why: The question says the internet side; wg0 is the inside of the tunnel.

prompt: Order the hops of pc1's traceroute to pc2 through the tunnel.
trap: 203.0.113.1 is not a hop at all: inside the tunnel the provider never appears.

prompt: A company with internet at both its sites wants the two LANs, on private addresses, to reach each other. What is the cheapest way?
hint: Use what is already paid for.

choices.text: A leased line between the two offices
choices.why: It works, and it is the expensive option the VPN section was avoiding.

choices.text: A site-to-site VPN between the routers
choices.why: Right. It rides on the connections both sites already have.

choices.text: Ask the provider to route 10.30.10.0/24
choices.why: No provider routes private ranges that thousands of companies reuse.

choices.text: One VLAN stretched across the two cities
choices.why: A VLAN divides switches; between cities something still has to carry the frames.
